title: The Creator Economy Is a Scam
summary: Two internet-culture journalists argue that content-creation coaching has become an MLM-style pyramid targeting stay-at-home mothers: resold AI-written courses, engagement pods, negligible platform payouts and a job far harder than pitched.

assertions.quote: Put this course back into chat GPT, make it your own, and then turn around and sell it to someone else.
And who's that most appealing to? The people who are staying home and raising their children.

verdicts.note: MLM participant surveys skew heavily toward women seeking flexible work, and the same demographic is targeted by creator-course marketing.

Only 16% of participants were stay-at-home parents when they joined; 40% were full-time employees seeking extra income, 12% students and 11% part-timers, so stay-at-home mothers are one target group, not the main one (60% of participants were women).

A reproduced MLM opportunity page pitches explicitly to 'a stay-at-home mom wanting to boost your budget' alongside professionals wanting to escape the nine-to-five; one example of the targeting, not a survey of it.

assertions.quote: The product is a placeholder to keep them out of legal hot water. What they're selling is opportunity.

verdicts.note: Income disclosures and regulator analyses show most MLM participants lose money once recruitment saturates.

91% of participants joined at least partly to make money and only 9% joined solely for the product discount, supporting the income pitch as the main draw; the product is not shown to be incidental (43% also wanted the discount).

At least 16 disclosures reclassify every zero-income participant as a customer or 'inactive' and six claim low earners joined just for discounts, with no basis given; this is the companies' framing of the product as the draw, which the FTC finds unsupported.

Taylor's analysis of 350 MLM pay plans concludes the defining flaw is an endless chain of recruiting participants as the primary customers, with plans that assume infinite and virgin markets that do not exist.

assertions.quote: you were very very much like first line and you probably got like you reaped the benefits of like a new world
$10.32 for generating like hundreds of thousands of views for that. Like I post every day on this platform.

verdicts.note: Creator-economy surveys find median earnings from platform programs are tiny; meaningful income comes from brand deals or owned products.

assertions.quote: a 30 second video is probably like four to five hours of work at the end of the day

verdicts.note: Creator time-use reports consistently show planning, filming and editing dominate, far beyond the posted runtime.

assertions.quote: the tech companies also they want you to spend more time on the app and they want you to create content for them

verdicts.note: Platforms do onboard new accounts into creator and bonus programs; the incentive is clear even if the motive is inferred.

assertions.quote: that is the least type of engaging content that you can possibly make

verdicts.note: Audience growth tracks a distinct topic or persona; meta-content about posting rarely builds a following.

assertions.quote: people that have almost no following that will create content for free in exchange for almost nothing

verdicts.note: UGC marketplaces and gifting-only campaigns are standard practice; pay is low or in-kind for small creators.

assertions.quote: that failure is a mindset problem rather than a structural inevitability
